item.title: NOTREKS: Improving Causal Discovery with Marginal Independence
item.description:
NOTREKS: Improving Causal Discovery with Marginal Independence

A new method for causal discovery, NOTREKS, has been introduced. It incorporates prior knowledge of marginally independent pairs of variables into score-based structure learning.

🔍 Overview

  • NOTREKS information is derived from the fact that marginally independent pairs of variables cannot be connected by a trek under faithfulness.
  • The method introduces a power-series trek (PSTrek) penalty for gradient-based optimization and a trek constraint for order-based search.

🧩 How it works

  • NOTREKS information helps in causal discovery by restricting the search space and improving both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification.
  • The method is tested on synthetic benchmarks with oracle NOTREKS information.

⚙️ Key details

  • The paper is titled “NOTREKS: Marginal Independence in Score-based Structure Learning” and was submitted on 18 Nov 2026.
  • The method is part of the Statistics > Machine Learning category on alphaXiv.

💡 Why it matters

  • The NOTREKS method can improve causal discovery by incorporating prior knowledge of marginally independent pairs of variables.
  • It can enhance both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification.

#CausalDiscovery #MachineLearning #Statistics #NOTREKS

Source: NOTREKS: Marginal Independence in Score-based Structure Learning

item.title: Locally Adaptive Neural Networks Achieve Optimal Performance
item.description:
Locally Adaptive Neural Networks Achieve Optimal Performance

A new approach to training neural networks, called locally adaptive neural networks, has been developed. This method addresses the limitations of globally fitted neural networks, which struggle with inhomogeneous regression functions that vary rapidly in some regions and are nearly flat in others.

🔍 Overview

  • Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space.
  • In regression problems, if the regression function is inhomogeneous, no single model can be appropriate everywhere, leading to degraded performance in regions where the function varies most rapidly.

🧩 How it works

  • Instead of fitting the network globally, the new approach fits it locally.
  • For each query point, a local neural network is trained on the k nearest-neighbours of that point alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent.

⚙️ Key details

  • The performance of the resulting estimator is analyzed through a localization approach.
  • The pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of k attains the rate n^{-2α/(2α+d*)}, up to logarithmic factors, when f0 is locally α-Hölder with α∈(0,1] and the covariates are supported on a d*-dimensional manifold embedded in ℝ^d.
  • A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal.
  • However, the local rate-optimality requires k to be calibrated to the smoothness of f0, which is unknown in practice.
  • A locally adaptive choice of k is provided to make the neural network adapt to the local Hölder exponent of f0 and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously.

💡 Why it matters

  • An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.

🚀 Availability

  • The paper “Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive” was submitted on 17 Nov 2026.
  • It is available in the Mathematics > Statistics Theory category on arXiv.

#NeuralNetworks #MachineLearning #Statistics #DataScience

Source: Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive

item.title: Rank-Induced Bias in LLM Leaderboards Can Systematically Overstate Top Model Performance
item.description:
Rank-Induced Bias in LLM Leaderboards Can Systematically Overstate Top Model Performance

Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. A new analysis reveals this “leaderboard winner’s curse” arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability — and the same selection effect distorts scores throughout the entire leaderboard, a phenomenon the authors term rank-induced bias.

🔍 The Problem

  • Reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated on public LLM leaderboards
  • Ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability
  • The same selection effect distorts scores throughout the leaderboard, not just at the top
  • Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile

🧩 How the Bootstrap Correction Works

The researchers develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap method to correct for this bias:

  • Assumes a fixed model pool with independently, identically distributed, bounded tasks
  • Allows arbitrary within-task correlation among models
  • Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, reduces $Θ(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$
  • Also quantifies confidence intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and groups models into tiers
  • Establishes sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers

⚙️ Key Results

Benchmark / Metric Finding
Scope of correction 14 benchmarks across 5 benchmark families
Magnitude of adjustment Rank-1 adjustments range from ~0.09 to 3.86 percentage points
SWE-bench Verified (tied leaders) Adjustment of 0.90 percentage points
Tier recovery (SWE-bench Verified) 13 of 173 models placed in the leading tier

Validation uses sample splitting and calibrated simulations.

🚀 Availability

The findings are combined in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER), which integrates both the score adjustment and the rank-interval tiers. The authors advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Systematic overstatement undermines confidence in leaderboard-based model comparisons
  • Even small adjustments (under 1 pp) can flip the apparent ranking of tied leaders
  • Tier-grouping gives a more honest picture of which models genuinely perform at the same level
  • Benchmark designers should account for selection effects and ranking uncertainty in future evaluations

#LLM #Leaderboards #Benchmarking #MachineLearning #Statistics #AISafety

Source: SOTA or Luck? The Winner’s Curse in LLM Leaderboards

item.title: StatFormBench: New Benchmark for Statistical Problem Formulation in LLMs
item.description:
StatFormBench: New Benchmark for Statistical Problem Formulation in LLMs

A new benchmark called StatFormBench has been released to evaluate how large language models handle the upstream step of statistical problem formulation.

🔍 Overview

  • The upstream step is formalized as Statistical Problem Formulation.
  • It is decomposed into two subtasks:
    1. Statistical Problem Classification
    2. Variable Identification & Role Assignment

🧩 How it works

Subtask What it involves
Statistical Problem Classification Assign a problem to a statistical category.
Variable Identification & Role Assignment Identify the relevant variables and their roles in the problem.

⚙️ Key details

  • StatFormBench is built from five cross‑domain statistics textbooks and a data‑science case library, covering diverse problem types, data representations, and scenario styles.
  • The benchmark contains 1,013 samples spanning 20 coarse‑grained and 85 fine‑grained statistical problem categories.
  • Evaluation across 14 open‑ and closed‑source LLMs shows:
    • Best zero‑shot classification accuracy: 72.0 % (fine‑grained).
    • Best variable set overlap: 63.2 %.
  • No single model dominates both subtasks, and enhanced prompting strategies give only limited or inconsistent improvements.

🚀 Availability

  • The benchmark data are released on Hugging Face.
  • Evaluation code is released on GitHub.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a standardized way to measure LLMs’ ability to parse and structure statistical problems before modeling.
  • Highlights current performance gaps, guiding future research on prompting techniques and model architectures for statistical reasoning.

#StatFormBench #LLM #Benchmark #Statistics #AI

Source: Benchmarking Language Models for Statistical Problem Formulation
